group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old man was driven to the emergency department by his spouse late this afternoon after complaining of two days of progressively thicker yellow sputum, low-grade fever, and a sense of “heaviness” in the chest that became pronounced whenever he walked from the living room to the kitchen. He lives in a single-story ranch house, mows his own lawn with frequent rests, and normally manages his medications and finances without assistance. His longstanding medical problems include a chronically reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction from ischemic cardiomyopathy—last transthoracic echo three months ago documented an EF of 30 %—and slowly worsening chronic kidney disease attributed to decades of hypertensive nephrosclerosis; serum creatinine has hovered around 2 mg/dL at primary-care visits, and he has never undergone dialysis. The heart-failure clinic recently titrated him to carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and torsemide 40 mg each morning, and a nephrologist added low-dose phosphate binder but no erythropoietin therapy. He has never been told he has cirrhosis, cancer, or prior stroke, and he denies residence in any long-term care facility. He quit smoking fifteen years earlier after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks a single beer with weekend dinners, and does not use illicit substances. Vaccination records on his phone confirm an inactivated influenza shot four months ago and a pneumococcal conjugate injection two years prior. His wife reports that on the drive he sat upright, conversed appropriately, and answered the day’s date correctly. They purposely avoided acetaminophen, inhalers, antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, or diuretics today so hospital staff could “see the real numbers.” On arrival the patient appeared tired but alert, speaking in full sentences with mild exertional pauses. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and without peripheral mottling; capillary refill was under two seconds. Untreated triage vitals recorded an oral temperature of 100.3 °F, regular pulse 81 beats per minute, automated blood pressure 91/54 mm Hg confirmed by repeat manual cuff, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute with shallow excursions, and fingertip pulse oximetry 93 % while breathing ambient air at this sea-level facility. Jugular venous distention rose to about 5 cm above the sternal angle while reclined at 45°, and there was trace pitting edema to the mid-shin bilaterally—unchanged from baseline per cardiology notes. Cardiac examination revealed a soft S3 with no new murmurs or rub; the PMI was laterally displaced. Lung examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right middle lobe anteriorly and the right lower posterior field, with resonant percussion throughout and no stony dullness or discrete shifting note to suggest free fluid. The abdomen was scaphoid, nontender, and without palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, clear speech, and symmetric 5/5 strength in all extremities. A bedside capillary glucose obtained before intravenous access measured 109 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of arrival—prior to any saline infusion—revealed sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 66 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL. Complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 14.2 × 10⁹/L with 89 % neutrophils, hematocrit 36 %, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. A right radial arterial sample obtained while he remained on room air returned pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 47 mm Hg, PaO₂ 81 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and base excess –4, consistent with a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis. Serum lactate was 2.1 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph, obtained before any medication or intravenous fluid, showed a dense homogeneous consolidation occupying the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; both costophrenic angles were sharply defined, the hemidiaphragms sat at normal height, and cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from an image six months earlier. No layering meniscus or blunting was visualized. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram displayed sinus rhythm at 80 beats per minute with Q waves in leads V1–V3 from prior infarction and no acute ST-T changes. Two peripheral blood-culture sets, an expectorated sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched before any antimicrobial, bronchodilator, vasopressor, diuretic, or antipyretic was administered. Up to the completion of this note the patient has received no intravenous fluids, oxygen, or medication other than minimal heparinized saline used to lock the arterial catheter, so all physiologic observations, laboratory values, and imaging findings above represent his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: for a man, start with age in years = 69. Not a nursing-home resident → 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure with EF 30% → 10; chronic kidney disease → 10. No reported malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: alert → 0; respiratory rate 25 (<30/min) → 0; systolic BP 91 (not <90 mm Hg) → 0; temperature 100.3°F (37.9°C, neither <35 nor ≥40°C) → 0; pulse 81 (<125/min) → 0.
- Laboratory and imaging: arterial pH 7.30 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 66 (≥30 mg/dL) → 20. Sodium 140 (not <130), glucose 109 (not ≥250 mg/dL), hematocrit 36% (not <30%), and room-air PaO₂ 81 (not <60 mm Hg) → 0 each. No pleural effusion → 0.
Sum: 69 + 10 + 10 + 30 + 20 = 139.
Final answer: 139
